item.title: Calgary home sales drop 15.3% in October: CREB
item.description: The number of homes that changed hands in Calgary last month dropped 15.3 per cent compared with October 2025 as prices ticked lower overall.
item.content:encoded: CALGARY — The number of homes that changed hands in Calgary last month dropped 15.3 per cent compared with October 2025 as prices ticked lower overall. The Calgary Real Estate Board says there were 1,592 home sales in October, as the residential benchmark price fell 0.4 per cent to $564,200. The board’s chief economist Ann-Marie Lurie says much of the pressure on pricing is concentrated in higher-density housing types due to oversupply, while detached and semi-detached prices have remained more stable. Apartment-style homes saw a year-over-year price decline of 7.9 per cent to $288,800, and row-style properties were 5.1 per cent less expensive at $407,500 last month. Detached home prices dipped 0.7 per cent to $735,100, while semi-detached prices moved 0.8 per cent higher compared with October 2025 to $685,200. There were 2,928 new listings on the market in October, down 9.4 per cent from a year earlier, while total inventory was 4.6 per cent lower year-over-year to 6,173 homes for sale. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

item.title: Meta delays new business terms after outcry over potential web scraping of news sites
item.description: Meta said it was postponing the rollout of new terms for its business accounts after an outcry from media companies and open-web advocates.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: Meta said it was postponing the rollout of new terms for its business accounts after an outcry from media companies and open-web advocates who said the updated rules would allow the tech giant to scrape vast amounts of data and potentially build competing services. The new rules, originally scheduled to go into effect Oct. 30, authorize Meta to use automated software such as web scrapers and bots to “index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs” associated with a business account. Critics say the update would have applied to all business clients, regardless of opposition, and without payment for the extracted content — and that Meta would have been able to use the content to potentially build products such as AI services that could compete with news publishers. Meta, however, said the update only applies to its ads and business products, and that how the company uses web crawlers is not changing. That said, regular users of Meta’s platforms, including Instagram and Facebook, can already have their posts scraped to train AI models as long as they are public. Opposition to Meta’s new terms is growing across Europe On Oct. 28, a court in Norway granted a temporary injunction suspending Meta’s new terms at the request of 180 Norwegian media companies, pending a full assessment of their legality. Their case was supported by the Norwegian Media Businesses’ Association (MBL), whose member newspapers account for approximately 97 per cent of Norwegian newspaper circulation. “We are satisfied that the court has agreed with us that Meta holds a dominant position in the relevant market and that the new terms are unreasonable,” said Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, MBL chair of the board. The U.K. Competition and Markets Authority said Oct. 30 it was starting its own investigation into the conditions. “The CMA is concerned that Meta requiring news publishers and other content businesses to accept these terms could amount to an unlawful imposition of unfair trading conditions,” it said Friday. Meta, however, says the terms don’t change how the company uses web crawlers. “This update is designed to make sure we’re able to pull accurate information about products for sale on third-party websites when making on-platform ad and content recommendations, not about scraping news sites,” wrote Meta spokesman Andy Stone on X on Oct. 16. His comments came after a report by the Nieman Journalism Lab at Harvard University, which said that as written, “the new terms could be used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products.” Nieman Lab said it consulted three legal experts who reviewed the terms at its request. While there do not appear to have been any lawsuits filed in the U.S., the Association of American Publishers called on Meta to drop the new terms. “In putting forth these onerous terms of service, Meta is implicitly acknowledging that permission is required for them to use creative works to develop and improve their products,” said Maria A. Pallante, AAP president and CEO, in a statement. “But at the same time this mega-corporation is abusing its dominant market power by compelling such consent from any commercial user who connects to any of their platforms.” At some point after Nieman Lab’s report, Meta removed the word “train” from the updated terms. The company says the update is not about scraping news sites. Meta on Oct. 29 said it was listening to feedback and said for now its existing terms remain in place. “We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” Stone posted on X. European critics say the changes made by Meta are not sufficient The Norwegian MBL said it wasn’t satisfied with the postponement and Meta’s assurances were insufficient. “This is about people’s access to trustworthy and critical journalism,” Randi S. Øgrey, CEO of the Norwegian MBL, said in a statement. “When the financial foundations of independent news media are weakened, media diversity and the democratic public sphere are at stake.” She said Norwegian media had three demands: Meta should commit in its new terms to respecting publishers’ reservations against scraping; using journalism in AI products should happen only after a separate, voluntary agreement and with payment; and publishers who do not sign the new terms should not be marginalized on Meta’s social platforms. The Movement for an Open Web, the group which originally complained to the CMA, called Meta’s move and the regulator’s investigation a “significant win,” but warned it was only the start. “Unless the CMA and other regulators make it abundantly and quickly clear that this sort of anti-competitive landgrab is not acceptable, then we will continue to see the tech giants throwing their weight around in this way,” said Tim Cowen from MOW. The European Union executive body, the European Commission, confirmed it had discussed the proposed new terms with Meta and welcomed the postponement of their entry into force. Spokesperson Sara Simonini said the commission was committed to ensuring that Meta’s practices comply with EU law, which prohibits a company from abusing its dominant market position and requires “gatekeeper” companies such as Meta to offer fair terms of use to businesses using their social platforms. Simonini also said the EU executive had asked unspecified providers of AI models to give details about what training material they use, in line with the EU’s new AI Act adopted in 2024 and currently being implemented. ___ Barbara Ortutay and Claudia Ciobanu, The Associated Press Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland.

item.title: No matter who controls congress, the need to reign in spending is critical: Larry Berman
item.description: Fiscal 2026 deficit was over US$2 Trillion as updated in the recent treasury statement. This week we find out how the Treasury will finance that debt.
item.content:encoded:
Fiscal 2026 deficit was over US$2 Trillion as updated in the recent treasury statement . This week we find out how the Treasury will finance that debt. The numbers are “dismal” in the words of the Congressional Budget Office. The U.S. spent more than $1 Trillion on interest costs alone. “America’s fiscal health is failing, and we need to take action to address it. In the year ahead, our leaders should avoid adding any new borrowing – on top of what we are already projected to – and commit to finding twice as many savings for every new must-have cost incurred.”

Percentage of GDP The biggest growth category of the deficit is the cost of financing it (pink area). While it’s true that cost of spending is income to the holders of the debt, and that money does get back into the economy, it takes away from other discretionary spending. Believe it or not, the U.S. government actually ran surpluses for several years during the internet birth and boom in the back half of the 1990s. In early 2000, the U.S. Treasury cancelled issuance of the long bond. Followed shortly after by massive tax cuts under Bush that ramped deficits again. It does not matter who is in the White House or Congress, they all spend our tax dollars rather poorly. Budget The average cost of financing that now $40 Trillion in debt is 3.518 per cent and rising quickly. This week, the U.S. Treasury will tell us their plans for financing over the next few quarters. The Quarterly Refunding Announcement and how they fund the deficit is important. Some are calling for them to cancel the 20-year issuance, others think they should add more bills over bonds at this point. Many will recall that my top pick back in mid-May was the U.S. long bond ETF looking out for 2027. So far, it’s been a volatile ride. Long bonds have the same standard deviation as the S&P 500 historically. If stocks are over valued and the economy is set to slow with gridlock in Washington, the U.S. Treasury will make moves to lower the long bond issuance, we will be right in the trade. iShares Related Stories Larry Berman: Geopolitical impacts short lived.
